Key audit · 525 Geni exports · 517,851 Wikidata Geni-ID statements

Every individual whose Geni ID is not a working key

The Geni profile ID is this project’s primary key, so a person whose key is wrong is a person no join will ever reach. This is the whole population of them, checked on both sides — the GEDCOM corpus and the local Wikidata store — and the count is not symmetric: the exports come back clean, and every genuinely broken key is on Wikidata.

31Wikidata items whose Geni ID field holds something that is not a Geni ID
70Geni profiles keyed to two Wikidata items at once
143Wikidata items caught in those double keyings
0broken keys in the GEDCOM corpus, over 2,281,820 individual records
35,098corpus individuals on a legacy ID shape — unusual, not broken

What “improperly keyed” was taken to mean

reading recorded
Taken
A key is improper when it cannot do a key’s job: the field holds something that is not a Geni profile ID, the two copies of the ID on one record disagree, one record carries no key, or one key is shared by two records that should be distinct. That is a property of the identifier, and it is checkable offline on both sides.
Rejected
“Any Geni ID that does not look like 6000000…”. It is the tempting reading — 35,098 corpus individuals fail it — but Wikidata’s own Geni ID statements carry 12,513 values in exactly those shapes, so they are older Geni IDs rather than bad ones. They are listed at the bottom of this page all the same, because they are the population the phrase might have meant.
What would switch it
A legacy-shaped ID that resolves to nothing on Geni. Settling that needs a live Geni lookup, which this project does not do on a whim.

Wikidata: 31 items whose Geni ID is not an ID

broken

Every one of these is a P2600 Geni.com profile ID statement whose value cannot be a profile ID. Most are a whole browser URL pasted into the identifier field, several still carrying the ?through= parameter Geni appends when you arrive from a relative’s page. Where a real ID is embedded in the mess it is recovered here; 7 of them contain no ID at all.

Wikidata: 70 Geni profiles keyed to two items each

broken

One Wikidata item carrying two Geni IDs is ordinary and correct — Geni holds unmergeable duplicate profiles, and a second P2600 is how you say so. This is the other direction, and it is not ordinary: one Geni profile claimed by two separate Wikidata items, 143 items in all. Either the two items are the same person and want merging, or one of them has the wrong ID on it. Read the labels side by side and it is usually obvious which.

The GEDCOM corpus: no broken keys at all

clean

Geni writes the profile ID twice on every individual — once as the record’s cross-reference, once as an RFN line — which makes the key self-checking. Every individual record in all 525 exports was read and put through the four checks below. Nothing failed any of them, so there is no such thing as an improperly keyed individual on the Geni side of this project.

The cross-reference is readable as a Geni ID

An xref outside the four record-type letters would parse to a fabricated ID pointing at a stranger’s profile — the failure this check exists for.

0 of 2,281,820
The cross-reference and the RFN agree

The two copies of the ID naming different profiles is the one fault that would silently merge two people into one.

0 of 2,281,820
Every individual carries an RFN

No record relies on the xref alone, so the cross-check is available everywhere.

0 missing
No key is used twice inside one export

Two individuals sharing a key in a single file would collapse to one on merge.

0 collisions

Corpus: 35,098 individuals on a legacy ID shape

unusual, not broken

Geni hands out nineteen-digit IDs opening 6000000, and 1,259,262 of the corpus’s 1,294,360 individuals have one. The rest do not, and the three shapes they take are listed below. They are almost certainly older allocations rather than errors: Wikidata’s Geni ID statements carry 2,074 short IDs, 3,647 eighteen-digit ones and 6,792 nineteen-digit ones that do not open 6000000, and Geni’s own relationship-path pages link them as live profiles. Search the table for a name, an ID, or a shape.

6,300Five to seven digits
10,102Eighteen digits
18,696Nineteen digits, not 6000000
Geni IDName as the export writes itShapeExports holding them

Built offline. The corpus figures come from a line scan of every .ged under exports/ that genimerge.sources counts as corpus — 525 files after byte-identical repeats are dropped. The Wikidata figures come from the local item store and its 517,851 Geni ID statements; nothing was asked of Wikidata live.

Absence is bounded in both directions. “Not sampled” means no export of ours has reached that person, never that Geni lacks them; and the store is a Geni-shaped slice of Wikidata, so a broken key outside it would not appear here.

Row data, every instance one row: reports/improper-keys-wikidata.csv (the 31), reports/shared-geni-keys.csv (the 143), reports/improper-keys.csv (the corpus scan). Built by scripts/scan-improper-keys.py and scripts/build-improper-keys-html.py.
